notes.headline: Venture Global: record LNG sales lift EPS to $0.96, nearly double forecasts; Plaquemines starts long-term contracts and EBITDA guidance jumps 14%
notes.takeaway: Revenue rose 43% to $4.8 billion and EPS of $0.96 was almost twice the $0.53 consensus as Venture Global sold 25% more LNG, much of it at spot prices. Plaquemines Phase 1 reached commercial operations on October 31, full-year EBITDA guidance rose to $10.0–$10.3 billion, and the shares jumped 7%.
results: Venture Global reported revenue of $4.8 billion for the third quarter, up 43%, and income from operations of $2.3 billion, up 74%. Net income attributable to shareholders rose almost sixfold to $2.5 billion, or $0.96 a share against $0.15 a year earlier, and consolidated adjusted EBITDA rose 69% to $2.6 billion. Year-to-date revenue was nearly $14 billion.

The company exported 124 cargoes and sold 465.8 trillion British thermal units of LNG, up 25%, from its Calcasieu Pass and Plaquemines plants in Louisiana. Plaquemines Phase 1 reached its commercial operations date on October 31, 2026, just over 53 months after the final investment decision, and began selling LNG to long-term contract customers.

Venture Global raised its 2026 consolidated adjusted EBITDA guidance to $10.0–$10.3 billion from $8.7–$9.1 billion. In October it signed frame agreements with GE Vernova and Baker Hughes for up to 16 new 720-megawatt power islands and related grid equipment.
mgmt: Chief executive Mike Sabel called it an exceptional quarter with record sales and earnings, LNG production at the high end of expectations and one of the fastest starts of long-term deliveries for a greenfield project of Plaquemines’ size. He said strong operations and the pricing outlook allowed the company to raise the midpoint of its volume and EBITDA guidance.

Sabel also described a potential new business: using the company’s experience building off-grid, island-mode power networks to offer an off-grid AI utility for data centres, combining power, land, closed-loop water, US natural gas supply and in-house engineering and construction.
view: Venture Global’s model has been both its strength and its controversy. It builds LNG plants faster and cheaper than rivals by using modular, factory-built trains, and it sells the gas produced during a long commissioning phase at high spot prices before switching to cheaper long-term contracts. That made the company enormously profitable in 2022–2025 and angered customers such as Shell and BP, who argued they should have received cargoes sooner. Plaquemines entering commercial operation is the turning point: from now on more of its output goes to contract customers at fixed fees, which lowers the upside from spot prices but makes earnings far more predictable.

This quarter shows how lucrative the commissioning phase was. EPS almost double the consensus reflects strong spot LNG prices and higher volumes, and the 14% increase in EBITDA guidance suggests the fourth quarter will also be strong. The transition matters for valuation: investors have discounted Venture Global for its legal disputes and its reliance on spot sales, and a steadier, contract-driven earnings stream could narrow that discount over time.

The data-centre idea is the wild card. Venture Global already operates its own gas-fired power plants to run its liquefaction facilities, and the GE Vernova and Baker Hughes agreements for up to 11.5 gigawatts of power equipment are serious hardware commitments. It is a logical extension, but it is also capital-hungry and unproven, coming from a company with substantial debt and the CP2 expansion still to fund. Investors should treat it as an option, not a plan, until a customer signs.
notes.watch: Watch the first full quarter of contract deliveries from Plaquemines, the outcome of remaining customer arbitrations, financing and progress at CP2, and whether a data-centre customer signs for off-grid power.
